example: New hires get training on the handbook, password managers, phishing and secure home Wi-Fi before receiving system access.
keyPoints: Eight listed topics; Should be role-based and repeated, not one-time; Measured through reporting and monitoring

definition: Training users on the organization's security policies and employee handbook so they know the rules and where to find them, often with a signed acknowledgement.
example: During onboarding, employees review the handbook's security section and sign that they understand the AUP.
category: 5.6 Security awareness > User guidance and training
keyPoints: Users cannot follow rules they do not know; Acknowledgement creates accountability; Update training when policies change; Keep policies easy to find (for example on the intranet) and track who has completed training

definition: Training users to stay alert to their surroundings and to security risks around them, such as shoulder surfing, tailgating, unknown people in secure areas, and suspicious devices.
example: An employee notices someone without a badge following them through a secure door and stops to ask for ID.
category: 5.6 Security awareness > User guidance and training
keyPoints: Be aware of people and physical surroundings, not just screens; Counters tailgating and shoulder surfing; Report suspicious activity; Applies online too: stay suspicious of unexpected links, attachments and text messages every day, not only during training

definition: Training users to understand that threats can come from people inside the organization, malicious or careless, and to recognize and report warning signs.
example: Staff learn that an unhappy coworker suddenly downloading customer lists before resigning is a warning sign to report.
category: 5.6 Security awareness > User guidance and training
keyPoints: Insiders already have access, which makes them dangerous; Signs: unusual access, data hoarding, disgruntlement; Pairs with least privilege and monitoring; Hard to detect, so use layers: multiple approvals for critical changes and file monitoring that alerts on changes

definition: Training users to create strong, unique passwords or passphrases, use a password manager, never share or reuse passwords, and use MFA.
example: Users are taught to store unique passwords in the company password manager instead of a sticky note.
category: 5.6 Security awareness > User guidance and training
keyPoints: Unique password per site prevents credential stuffing; Password managers and MFA; Never share credentials, even with IT; Rules can also be enforced technically, for example with Windows Group Policy

definition: Training users not to plug in unknown USB drives, cables or chargers, because they can carry malware or act as malicious devices, and to follow rules for approved media.
example: An employee finds a USB drive labeled "Salaries" in the parking lot and hands it to IT instead of plugging it in.
category: 5.6 Security awareness > User guidance and training
keyPoints: Baiting with dropped USB drives is a common attack; Malicious cables can act as keyboards or exfiltrate data; Use only approved, encrypted media

definition: Training users to recognize manipulation tactics such as pretexting, impersonation, phishing, vishing, smishing, tailgating and urgency, and to verify requests before acting.
example: A caller claiming to be the CEO asks for an urgent wire transfer; the employee calls the CEO back on a known number to verify.
category: 5.6 Security awareness > User guidance and training
keyPoints: Attackers exploit trust, authority and urgency; Verify through a separate trusted channel; Covers email, phone, text and in-person attacks

definition: Training users to protect sensitive information in daily activity, such as not posting work details online, keeping a clean desk, and not discussing confidential matters in public.
example: An employee avoids posting a photo of their desk because the monitor shows internal project names and a login screen.
category: 5.6 Security awareness > User guidance and training
keyPoints: OPSEC = do not leak information through normal behavior; Social media posts can help attackers; Clean desk and screen locking; Think like an attacker: what could someone learn from what I share?

definition: Training users on working securely outside the office: using the VPN, securing home Wi-Fi, avoiding public networks, protecting devices and screens from others, and keeping work and personal use separate.
example: A remote worker connects through the company VPN and uses a privacy screen when working in a coffee shop.
category: 5.6 Security awareness > User guidance and training
keyPoints: Home and public networks are less trusted; Use VPN, updates and strong Wi-Fi security; Watch for shoulder surfing and family use of work devices

definition: Measuring and reporting how well the awareness program works, through initial (baseline) and recurring measurements such as phishing click rates, report rates and training completion.
example: The program reports a 30% click rate at launch and 8% after a year of training.
keyPoints: Two listed: initial and recurring; Metrics prove effectiveness and guide changes; Track both failures (clicks) and good behavior (reports)

definition: The first measurement taken when an awareness program starts, setting a baseline to compare future results against.
example: Before any training, a phishing simulation shows 30% of staff click, which becomes the baseline.
keyPoints: Baseline = starting point; Needed to show improvement later; Compare recurring = ongoing measurement; Some study sources read "initial" at the user level instead: the first time a person does something risky, the response is training

definition: Regular, ongoing measurement and reporting of awareness results over time, such as monthly phishing metrics and training completion rates.
example: Each month the security team reports phishing click and report rates to management to track trends.
keyPoints: Shows trends and whether training works; Finds departments or users needing more help; Compare initial = one baseline measurement; At the user level, recurring means the same person repeats the behavior, which signals they need more help

definition: Creating the awareness program: assessing needs, setting goals, identifying audiences and roles, choosing topics and formats, and building the content.
example: The team surveys staff, sees remote work risks are high, and builds short monthly videos and a phishing program aimed at each department.
keyPoints: Development = plan and build; Tailor content to roles and risks; Set measurable goals before launch; Often built by a dedicated awareness team; content can be tailored to job functions and compliance needs

definition: Delivering the awareness program: rolling out training, running campaigns, scheduling sessions, tracking participation and adjusting based on results.
example: Training launches company-wide in January, phishing simulations run monthly, and managers get completion reports.
keyPoints: Execution = deliver and run; Track completion and results; Feeds back into development to improve the program; Delivered online or in person; metrics go to managers and IT to show how controls perform
